https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c39e.text: Image source, Kiama Council Image caption, A former apprentice stonemason who helped build the Houses of Parliament is thought to have borrowed the book in the late 1800s By Lana Lam Sydney Published 7 August 2026 A book borrowed 150 years ago has finally been returned to an Australian library, with the culprit linked to the Houses of Parliament in London. Antiquities of Athens was borrowed from a local library in Kiama, a seaside town about 120km (75 miles) south of Sydney, some time in the mid-1870s. The book on classic Greek architecture was stored in a tea chest hidden behind a boarded-up fireplace for decades before it was recently discovered by a family member. Ross Simmons, 77, thinks his great-grandfather, John Simmons, might have borrowed the book to help with his career, having worked as an apprentice stonemason in Westminster in the mid-1800s before becoming an architect in Australia. Image source, Kiama Council Image caption, The book was a little water damaged but otherwise in a good condition Simmons, a self-confessed family history buff, said his great-grandfather studied in London between 1839 to 1844. "After his studies in London, he was apprenticed to other stonemasons to help in the construction of the Houses of Parliament," Simmons said. In 1857, aged 27, John Simmons emigrated from the UK to Australia, first living in the Sydney suburb of Newtown before relocating to Kiama after leading the construction of a sandstone church in the coastal town. "He had quite an interest in architecture, construction and building," Simmons said, adding that the overdue book "probably sat on a shelf at his house" and was used as a reference. The book somehow ended up in a tea chest - along with other family records - which was placed in a fireplace that was covered up. Image source, Supplied: Jo Hartmann Image caption, The fireplace where the book was found had been sealed for decades About 30 years ago, the tea chest was uncovered during renovations and the books - including the overdue one - were given to Simmons for safekeeping. But it wasn't until about a fortnight ago that he went through some of the books in greater detail. "I looked inside the front cover and, lo and behold, on the second page there was a Kiama Library stamp," Simmons said, with the library's borrowing conditions also detailed on the inside cover. For instance, library members could only borrow one book at a time, unless it could be proved that six people in the same household could read, in which case, three books could be lent out. Anyone intoxicated was barred from borrowing and members returning books past their due date would be fined three pence for every week it was late. Kiama Library staff worked out that the fine would be Â£97 - or in today's currency AU$28,000 ($20,000; Â£15,000), allowing for inflation. But luckily for the Simmons family, the fine has been waived. Kiama Council libraries manager Michelle Hudson said the unusual find had attracted a lot of attention. Image source, Jane Thompson Image caption, Kiama Council libraries manager Michelle Hudson said people have travelled from out of town to come and see the book "People have travelled 40 minutes away to come and actually hold the book... it's a beautiful little book and it's got an amazing story to tell," she said. The cloth-bound volume has some water damage but otherwise, is in good condition, Hudson said. "It does have beautiful illustrations in it and some pages that fold out to show you they were using exact measurements of some of the monuments in Greece." She said in 1872, the council got a Â£200 grant to establish the town's library and and it had fewer than 1,000 books in its collection, with the overdue book marked as number 506. Image source, Catherine Taylor Image caption, The book, published in 1858, features Greek monument illustrations that fold out There's no way to know exactly who borrowed the book or when, Hudson said, as the library's borrowing records from that period have since been lost. However, the book is no longer available to borrow, having been added to the library's collection of special items, which can be viewed on request. "It won't be able to go out again... we don't want to wait another 150 years for it to come back," Hudson joked. As for the book's much-delayed return, Simmons said he believes his great-grandfather would be pleased with the final chapter of its journey. "I think he'd be happy to see the book returned and he'd probably have a bit of a laugh about it." Longtime ​Slovak leader Fico, who has kept up warm relations with Russia ‌and refuses military aid for Ukraine, said this week that Europe was closer than ever to a large-scale war erupting from the Ukraine war. At the same time, some European leaders, such as those in France and Poland, have warned of Russian hybrid attacks. In ‌his ​video message, Fico said, “We face a mortal danger” ⁠while watching the West “pour fuel ⁠on the fire” with its support for Ukraine, which he said had been to no avail. “The failure of the strategy to destroy Russia through the war in Ukraine has led some Western politicians to believe ​that if the goal cannot be achieved through the Ukrainian army and full support for it, then every effort must be made to trigger ⁠a conflict between NATO and Russia,” Fico ⁠said in the video posted on social media. He said the ​war in Ukraine was not Slovakia’s nor NATO’s war but said, “Certain war hawks ​within NATO are trying, at any cost, to turn this ‌war into a conflict between Russia and NATO.” Earlier this week, Fico warned a drone incursion could spark the activation of NATO’s collective defence clause and he wanted to prevent Slovakia — which neighbours Ukraine and is a member of ⁠the NATO military alliance — from becoming part of an armed conflict. He said on Saturday that creating a pretext to start a war was easy and reiterated ⁠Slovakia would not send ‌soldiers to fight under a fabricated pretext. French President Emmanuel ⁠Macron said on Friday that Russia was intensifying its ​campaign of ‌hybrid attacks against Europe, and he cited an attempted ​drone attack ⁠at Leipzig airport in August, which the German government concluded Moscow was behind, as evidence of the changing nature of Russian aggression. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday, citing unnamed intelligence agencies, that Russia plans to launch hybrid drone and missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine. https://www.baltictimes.com/signals_from.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Signals from Brussels on anti-drone funding are positive - Lithuanian defense minister 2026-09-28 LETA/BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - Lithuania's Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said on Monday that signals from Brussels on additional European Commission funding for anti-drone defenses were positive, after the Baltic states requested urgent financial support. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia on Monday appealed to the European Commission for an urgent allocation of 500 million euros to bolster their anti-drone capabilities. According to Kaunas, the Baltic states' priority is air defense, with Lithuania focusing primarily on drone detection and kinetic capabilities. The minister said the Commission would consider the request, with the specific purpose of the funding to be defined during negotiations. The countries hope the European Union can provide additional funding for regional drone defense as early as 2026. Sources suggest that strengthening anti-drone defenses is an urgent matter, as Russia may seek to test NATO's Article 5 with drone attacks against the Alliance's eastern flank. "Russia will certainly not stop; its entire economy today is a war economy. Even if a ceasefire or peace is reached, Russia will still produce weaponry. (...) This means our defense industry must move forward even faster. When we have negotiating agreements with various manufacturers today, we are usually talking not about quantities, but about deadlines. Manufacturers, unfortunately, put everything into a very long queue; lead times are long, instead of us receiving the ordered production faster," Kaunas said. "By having a strong army and strong weaponry on our lands, we will certainly deter Russia," he added. Comments Related Articles Subscribe Log In Ads Please enter your username and password. History Hangs Heavily in the ‘City of Saints’ COMMENTARY: The Nov. 7 shooting in Kraków hits close to home. A woman places candle in an improvised memorial next to St. Mary's Basilica in Kraków on Nov. 9, 2026, two days after a deadly shooting. (Photo: Omar Marques / Getty Images) Father Raymond J. de Souza Commentaries November 13, 2026 If circumstances permit a pilgrim to travel, there are three essential cities for Catholics: Jerusalem, where the history of salvation unfolded; Rome, where the history of the Church unfolded; and Kraków, where the history of our time unfolded. Nov. 7’s mass shooting, leaving six random people dead and 16 wounded — the shooter himself died after exchanging gunfire with police — was another manifestation of how heavily history hangs in the City of Saints. The shooting hit close to home for me and my colleagues in the Tertio Millennio Seminar on the Free Society , which has taken place in Kraków every summer since 1994. I was a student in the first Cracovian seminar, spending three marvelous weeks in one of the jewels in the crown of European royal capitals, and have returned as a member of the faculty most summers since 2009. Stephen White, executive director of the Saint John Paul II National Shrine in Washington, D.C., and I live in the same university student residence when we are there, just down the block from where the murderous rampage ended on Saturday. We walk past that exact spot on our way to breakfast each morning, a place now marked, as Stephen has written , by horror and heroism. In his book for Kraków’s World Youth Day in 2016, George Weigel, an original faculty member and leader of the seminar for more than 25 years, focused on the holy history of Kraków, hence the title “City of Saints.” But the book opens by noting the wider history, namely that Kraków is the “city where the twentieth century happened.” And, one might now add, the 21st century, too. At the time that Weigel’s book came out, I traced some of that history. The 20th century opened with Kraków, city of Polish kings, belonging to the Habsburg Empire. Poland had been erased from the map of Europe at the end of the 18th century. St. John Paul the Great was named “Karol” after the last Habsburg emperor, Blessed Karl of Austria, in whose armed forces his father served. In his last beatification ceremony in 2004, John Paul beatified Karl, “my father’s emperor.” The Polish nation, deprived of the instruments of sovereignty for more than a century, relied upon its spiritual and cultural heritage to sustain itself: the legacy of the kings buried in Wawel Cathedral of Kraków, and the relics of St. Stanislaus, the martyr-bishop, at Skałka, a short walk down from Wawel Hill. That challenge of sustaining a nationality without a nation-state — defining a nation by culture rather than political sovereignty — would give shape to much of 20th-century geopolitics and national liberation movements. The greatest of those liberation movements, the peaceful defeat of communism, had its spiritual origins in Kraków, the city that both St. Faustina Kowalska and John Paul moved to in the 1930s. The Auschwitz martyrs, St. Maximilian Kolbe and St. Teresa Benedicta of the Cross, were killed in what was then the Kraków Archdiocese. Two world wars, national independence, invasion by neighbors — first the Soviets (1920) and then the Nazis and the Soviets (1939) — and the Cold War; all of it took place in Kraków, which in turn provided the man of the century, Karol Józef Wojtyła. The great questions after the defeat of the Soviet empire were taken up in Poland with particular intensity. On what basis should a free society be built? What kind of culture is required to sustain a free politics and a free economy? What did it mean for Poland to rejoin Europe, and how did Europe understand its own identity? To what extent did the great postwar European institutions — the European Union and NATO — provide for the peace and prosperity of its peoples? The 21st-century project would unfold with Poland as protagonist, too. When Russia expanded its war against Ukraine in 2022, Cracovians were immediately engaged, just a few hundred kilometers from the Ukrainian border. Despite serious tensions between Poles and Ukrainians in the past century, Ukrainian refugees were welcomed into family homes. There were no refugee camps. While some of Ukraine’s allies have since betrayed it, Poland has been steadfast. Thus it seems somehow sadly fitting that there would be a mass shooting in the heart of Kraków. While Americans are long accustomed to domestic terrorism (Oklahoma City) and even school shootings have become frequent, in Poland such violence is utterly novel. The main market square in Kraków, where the shooting began, is one of the grandest and happiest public spaces anywhere. Lethal violence invaded that space, as the hurts of history always do in Kraków. St. Mary’s Basilica in the square might be thought of as the spiritual heart of Kraków, while Wawel Cathedral is its head. The shooting spree passed in front of the basilica, where from the tower, every hour on the hour, a trumpeter plays a five-note bugle call, the Hejnał Mariacki , to each of the four directions. It ends abruptly, without a proper conclusion. Tradition holds that it commemorates a trumpeter long ago warning of invaders approaching; an arrow killed him while he was sounding the alarm. The Hejnał Mariacki was suspended for 12 hours after the shooting, a moment of silence for a city accustomed to many moments of common grief. It resumed, continuing as it has for more than six centuries. It summons the city to rise and serenades it to sleep, interrupted by the arrow of hatred, aimed so often at the heart of Poland and its ancient and royal capital.
